steps.text: Part 3 of 4: Double check: how to see it, set it up and stop it. This part covers Set one up, stop one; Look-alikes and a mixed test; Mixed test. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Setting one up, and stopping one.** [I] Two ways to set one up, from the boards in this lesson: put a long-range piece behind a piece that has a checking square, or use a first check to drive the king onto the line. Dan Heisman advises listing the opponent's checks, captures and threats before each move [S, paraphrased]. [I] The question this theme adds: does an enemy long-range piece stand behind a piece that could check my king?

steps.caption: Black to move. No double check exists yet. The queen on c5 aims along a diagonal at g1, and no black long-range piece aims at h1 yet. A first check can change that.

line.say: A single check, from a knight that also blocks the queen's diagonal. The king has one move.
The king has only one move, g1: onto the queen's diagonal.
Now the knight checks again as it unblocks the diagonal: a double check.
The king has other moves (h1 or f1); every one loses to mate. After f1, the queen mates on f2.
The queen mates on f2, protected by the knight on h3.

claims.statement: After the first three moves, two black pieces attack the king on g1.
Black forces mate within three moves.
The first check is the engine's first choice (depth 16).

steps.caption: White to move. The knight on e5 stands between the rook's file and the king on e7: no double check exists yet. A quiet rook move can set one up.

line.say: A quiet move: the rook goes behind the knight. If Black ignores it, White has a double check.
Black plays a move that does not meet the threat.
The knight checks and uncovers the rook: two checks, no square for the king, mate. [V] The engine's best defence is the king stepping off the file, and White is still about four pawns up.

claims.statement: The quiet rook move is the engine's first choice (depth 16).
After the quiet move no white piece attacks the king yet: the knight blocks the rook.
If Black ignores it, two white pieces attack the king after the knight jump.

steps.caption: White to move. The same placement as the earlier rook-and-knight board, but now White is to move: what would Black threaten if White passed? The king on g3 and the rook on c3 share a rank, and Black's knight is between them.

line.say: The king leaves the third rank. A jump by the knight cannot uncover the rook any more.
The knight still gives a check.
But it is a single check, and the king walks away.

claims.statement: If White passed, Black's knight capture would win material.
Several king moves are within 40 hundredths of the best (depth 16).
After the knight check, only one black piece attacks the king.

steps.caption: The same position. What if White ignores the line and moves the king along the rank?

line.say: The king stays on the third rank.
The knight takes the pawn. It does not attack f3, so this is a single discovered check.
The knight takes the rook again.

claims.statement: The king move is at least four pawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
After the knight capture, only the rook attacks the king on f3.

steps.text: **Many defences work.** [V] At depth 16 the engine rates stepping the king off the rank, advancing a pawn and capturing with the rook within about a pawn of each other. What fails is leaving the king on the line. [I] So ask before each move: does an enemy long-range piece stand behind a piece that could check me? The king, the back piece or the front piece can move, or the line can be blocked.

**Two look-alikes and one failed double check.** (1) The line is blocked, so the move gives one check. (2) The front piece lands where it does not attack the king: a *discovered* check, which can be blocked. And a real double check can still fail: the king takes the checker, or has a safe square (the third condition). Ask: which check is missing, or which king answer exists?

steps.caption: A bare board, White to move. The bishop again blocks the rook's file, and Black has a rook on b6.

line.say: The bishop uncovers the rook, but from g3 it does not attack the king: a single check.
A single check allows a block. Black puts the rook on the file.

claims.statement: After the bishop moves, only one white piece attacks the king.

steps.title: Is the checker safe from the king?
steps.prompt: All three positions hold the same bishop move with two checks. In the second, the white pawn on c5 is missing. In the third, Black's a-pawn has moved. Predict which are checkmate.
Six positions, unlabelled. Which kind did you miss: a double check you did not see, or a look-alike you believed? Six positions are too few to prove anything, so treat this as a note.

fields.label: I mostly missed:
options: a double check I did not see
a real double check that fails, which I thought won
neither, or I am not sure

steps.text: **Remember.** Before each move, ask: does an enemy long-range piece stand behind a piece that could check my king? If yes, move the king, move either piece, or block the line. A blocked line or a front piece that does not check is only a look-alike.
